questions.name: Two Sum
questions.description: Given an array of numbers and a target number, find the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
questions.interviewQuestion: Can you find two numbers in an array that add up to a target sum in a single pass without using nested loops?
questions.hint: As you walk through the array, calculate the missing partner number needed to reach the target, then check if you've already saved that partner in a map.
commonMistakes: Using the same element at an index twice
Using two nested loops leading to an inefficient O(n^2) solution
followUpQuestions: What if the array is already sorted?
What if you need to return all unique pairs instead of just one?

questions.name: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
questions.description: Given an array of stock prices where each element is the price on a given day, find the maximum profit you can make by buying on one day and selling on a future day.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you calculate the maximum single-transaction profit in a line of daily stock prices using only one pass?
questions.hint: Keep track of the lowest price seen so far as you move forward, and compare the profit you would get if you sold today against your max profit.
commonMistakes: Trying to sell before buying (moving backward in time)
Comparing every possible pair of buy/sell days with nested loops
followUpQuestions: What if you are allowed to buy and sell as many times as you want?
What if there is a transaction fee for every trade?

questions.name: Contains Duplicate
questions.description: Given an array of integers, check if any value appears at least twice in the array.
questions.interviewQuestion: How can you quickly determine if an array contains duplicate elements?
questions.hint: Store each number in a Hash Set as you visit it; if you encounter a number already in the set, a duplicate exists.
commonMistakes: Comparing every pair of numbers with nested loops
Sorting the array first when a faster hash set solution exists (unless space is strictly limited)
followUpQuestions: What if space complexity must be kept at O(1)?
What if duplicates must be within k positions of each other?

questions.name: Product of Array Except Self
questions.description: Given an array, return a new array where each element at index i is equal to the product of all numbers in the original array except the one at i, without using division.
questions.interviewQuestion: Can you compute the product of all elements except the current one without using division and in linear time?
questions.hint: Calculate the cumulative product of all numbers to the left of each index in a first pass, then multiply by the cumulative product of all numbers to the right in a second pass.
commonMistakes: Using division, which breaks when zero is in the array and violates problem rules
Creating full extra left and right arrays when the answer array can be updated in place
followUpQuestions: Can you solve this with O(1) extra memory space (excluding the output array)?
How would you handle matrix multiplication variants of this problem?

questions.name: Maximum Subarray
questions.description: Given an integer array, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) which has the largest sum and return its sum.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the contiguous group of numbers that yields the maximum possible sum in linear time?
questions.hint: At each position, decide whether to add the current number to your ongoing sum or drop the previous sum and start fresh from the current number.
commonMistakes: Resetting the current sum to 0 instead of restarting from the current negative element
Not handling arrays that consist entirely of negative numbers
followUpQuestions: Can you also return the starting and ending indices of the maximum subarray?
How would you approach this using a Divide and Conquer approach?

questions.name: Maximum Product Subarray
questions.description: Given an integer array, find a contiguous non-empty subarray that has the largest product and return that product.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you handle negative numbers when searching for the contiguous subarray with the maximum product?
questions.hint: Keep track of both the maximum product AND the minimum product so far, because multiplying a negative minimum by another negative number turns it into a positive maximum.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to swap current max and current min when encountering a negative number
Assuming the maximum product will always be positive
followUpQuestions: What happens if zeroes are present in the array?
How does this change if you need to return the actual elements producing the product?

questions.name: Merge Sorted Array
questions.description: Given two sorted integer arrays, merge the second array into the first array as one sorted array in-place.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you merge two sorted arrays into one in-place without needing extra storage space?
questions.hint: Start comparing elements from the end of both arrays and place the larger element at the back of the first array to avoid overwriting existing data.
commonMistakes: Merging from the front, which forces you to shift existing elements repeatedly
Forgetting to process remaining elements in the second array after the first array finishes
followUpQuestions: How would you merge k sorted arrays simultaneously?
What if the arrays were stored as linked lists instead?

questions.name: Move Zeroes
questions.description: Given an integer array, move all 0s to the end while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements in-place.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you shift all zero values to the end of an array without changing the order of non-zero numbers or allocating extra memory?
questions.hint: Use a write pointer to keep track of where the next non-zero element should go, swapping non-zero numbers forward as you find them.
commonMistakes: Creating a copy of the array instead of modifying it in-place
Swapping elements without preserving the relative order of non-zero numbers
followUpQuestions: How can you minimize the total number of write operations if the array has mostly zeroes?
What if you need to move a specific value other than zero?

questions.name: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
questions.description: Given a sorted array, remove duplicates in-place such that each unique element appears only once, returning the new length.
questions.interviewQuestion: How can you remove duplicate elements from a pre-sorted array in O(1) extra space?
questions.hint: Maintain a slow pointer for unique positions; move a fast pointer across the array, updating the slow pointer position whenever a new unique value is seen.
commonMistakes: Not taking advantage of the fact that the input array is already sorted
Using extra memory like a set when in-place modification is required
followUpQuestions: What if duplicates are allowed to appear at most twice instead of once?
How would you adapt this if the array was not sorted initially?

questions.name: Rotate Array
questions.description: Given an integer array, rotate the array to the right by k steps, where k is non-negative.
questions.interviewQuestion: How can you rotate an array by k positions in-place using constant memory?
questions.hint: Reverse the entire array, then reverse the first k elements, and finally reverse the remaining elements.
commonMistakes: Not taking k modulo array length (k = k % n), leading to redundant rotations
Using extra array memory when an in-place reversal strategy works in linear time
followUpQuestions: Can you solve this using cyclic replacements instead of array reversals?
How would you handle rotating a 2D matrix instead of a 1D array?

questions.name: Majority Element
questions.description: Given an array of size n, find the element that appears more than ⌊n / 2⌋ times.
questions.interviewQuestion: How can you find the element that appears more than half the time in an array using O(1) extra space?
questions.hint: Use a voting strategy: maintain a candidate and a counter. Increment the counter when you see the candidate, decrement when you see a different number, and pick a new candidate when the counter hits zero.
commonMistakes: Using a hash map to count frequencies when constant extra space is requested
Sorting the array first, which takes O(n log n) time instead of linear O(n) time
followUpQuestions: What if you need to find all elements that appear more than ⌊n / 3⌋ times?
How would you handle a stream of data where elements arrive dynamically?

questions.name: Missing Number
questions.description: Given an array containing n distinct numbers in the range [0, n], return the only number in the range that is missing from the array.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find a single missing number in an unsorted array of consecutive integers from 0 to n in O(n) time and O(1) space?
questions.hint: Calculate the expected total sum using the arithmetic series formula n * (n + 1) / 2, then subtract the actual sum of the array elements.
commonMistakes: Sorting the array to find gaps, which degrades time complexity to O(n log n)
Potential integer overflow if using sum in languages with fixed-size integers (can be avoided using XOR)
followUpQuestions: How would you solve this using XOR operations to completely prevent integer overflow?
What if two numbers were missing instead of just one?

questions.name: Find the Duplicate Number
questions.description: Given an array of integers containing n + 1 integers where each integer is in the range [1, n] inclusive, find the duplicate number without modifying the array and using constant space.
questions.interviewQuestion: How can you detect a duplicate number in an immutable array where values act as pointers?
questions.hint: Treat the array as a linked list where values represent indices pointing to the next node. Use Floyd's Cycle Detection (slow and fast pointers) to find where the cycle begins.
commonMistakes: Modifying the array (e.g., sorting or sign marking) when constraints prohibit array modification
Using a set or hash map, which violates the O(1) extra space constraint
followUpQuestions: What if there are multiple duplicate numbers present?
How would you solve this if you were allowed to modify the array in-place?

questions.name: Sort Colors
questions.description: Given an array with n objects colored red, white, or blue (represented as 0, 1, and 2), sort them in-place so that objects of the same color are adjacent, in the order red, white, and blue.
questions.interviewQuestion: Can you sort an array containing only 0s, 1s, and 2s in a single pass without using built-in sort functions?
questions.hint: Use three pointers (low, mid, high). Move 0s to the low boundary and 2s to the high boundary while scanning through with mid.
commonMistakes: Advancing the mid pointer after swapping with high without re-evaluating the new mid element
Using a two-pass counting sort when a single-pass solution is requested
followUpQuestions: How would you generalize this algorithm to sort k distinct colors or categories?
How would you adapt this to separate negative, zero, and positive numbers?

questions.name: Merge Intervals
questions.description: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], merge all overlapping intervals, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you combine overlapping time intervals into a clean, consolidated list?
questions.hint: Sort the intervals by their start times first. Then iterate through, comparing the start time of the current interval with the end time of the last merged interval.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to sort intervals before attempting to merge them
Overwriting start times instead of updating end times to max(end1, end2)
followUpQuestions: How do you process a new interval added dynamically into an already merged list?
What if intervals are given as continuous streams?

questions.name: Insert Interval
questions.description: Given a set of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start time, insert a new interval into the intervals (merge if necessary).
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you efficiently insert a new time interval into an already sorted list of non-overlapping intervals?
questions.hint: Divide the process into three phases: append non-overlapping intervals before the new one, merge all overlapping intervals into the new one, and then append remaining intervals after.
commonMistakes: Re-sorting the whole array when it is already sorted, degrading performance to O(n log n)
Failing to update both start and end boundaries when merging overlapping intervals
followUpQuestions: Can you implement this using binary search to quickly pinpoint insertion positions?
How does this extend to finding interval intersections?

questions.name: Set Matrix Zeroes
questions.description: Given an m x n integer matrix, if an element is 0, set its entire row and column to 0s in-place.
questions.interviewQuestion: How can you mark and zero out entire rows and columns in a 2D matrix without using extra memory?
questions.hint: Use the first row and first column of the matrix itself as storage to flag which rows and columns need to be zeroed out.
commonMistakes: Zeroing out cells immediately during the first pass, causing subsequent checks to read false zeroes
Not handling the first row and first column flags separately before overriding them
followUpQuestions: What if you are only allowed to modify the matrix once (single pass)?
How would you optimize this if the matrix was sparse?

questions.name: Spiral Matrix
questions.description: Given an m x n matrix, return all elements of the matrix in spiral order.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you traverse a 2D matrix in a clockwise spiral pattern from the outside in?
questions.hint: Maintain four boundary pointers (top, bottom, left, right) and shrink them inward after traversing each edge.
commonMistakes: Re-traversing single remaining rows or columns when top > bottom or left > right during middle checks
Off-by-one errors on grid boundary transitions
followUpQuestions: How would you generate an n x n matrix filled with numbers from 1 to n^2 in spiral order?
How do you traverse a 3D grid in spiral layer order?

questions.name: Rotate Image
questions.description: Given an n x n 2D matrix representing an image, rotate the image by 90 degrees (clockwise) in-place.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you rotate an n x n matrix by 90 degrees clockwise without allocating another matrix?
questions.hint: First transpose the matrix (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]), then reverse each row horizontally.
commonMistakes: Transposing full rows twice and accidently reverting back to the original matrix
Creating a temporary output matrix, violating the constant space requirement
followUpQuestions: How would you rotate the matrix 90 degrees counter-clockwise?
How would you rotate a non-square m x n matrix in-place?

questions.name: Container With Most Water
questions.description: Given n non-negative integers representing vertical lines, find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container that holds the most water.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you maximize the area bounded by two lines in linear time?
questions.hint: Place pointers at both ends of the array. Calculate area, then move the pointer pointing to the shorter height inward, as that's the only way to potentially increase the area.
commonMistakes: Moving the taller line pointer instead of the shorter one
Checking every pair of lines using nested loops, which takes O(n^2) time
followUpQuestions: What if you need to find a container with 3 lines or walls?
How does this problem change if the container bottom is not flat?

questions.name: Trapping Rain Water
questions.description: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you calculate the total trapped rainwater across an elevation map in linear time and constant space?
questions.hint: The water trapped above any bar depends on the minimum of the highest bar to its left and the highest bar to its right. Use two pointers moving inward, keeping track of leftMax and rightMax.
commonMistakes: Using O(n) extra space for precomputed left/right max arrays when two pointers achieve O(1) space
Forgetting that water height is bounded by the smaller of the two maximum heights
followUpQuestions: How would you solve this problem in 2D for a grid/matrix terrain?
How would you adapt the algorithm if the bar width varies?

questions.name: Next Permutation
questions.description: Rearrange numbers into the lexicographically next greater permutation of numbers. If such an arrangement is impossible, rearrange it as the lowest possible order.
questions.interviewQuestion: How can you find the next lexicographical permutation of an array in-place without generating all permutations?
questions.hint: Find the first decreasing element from the right, swap it with the smallest element to its right that is larger than it, and reverse the remaining sequence to its right.
commonMistakes: Generating all permutations using recursion, leading to O(n!) time complexity
Forgetting to handle the edge case where the array is sorted in descending order
followUpQuestions: How would you find the previous permutation instead of the next?
How many total unique permutations exist if the array contains duplicate numbers?

questions.name: Pascal's Triangle
questions.description: Given an integer numRows, return the first numRows of Pascal's triangle.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you construct Pascal's Triangle up to n rows iteratively?
questions.hint: Each row starts and ends with 1. Every middle element at index j is the sum of elements at index j-1 and j from the previous row.
commonMistakes: Out-of-bounds array access when calculating edge elements (1s)
Recomputing row values recursively instead of building them iteratively
followUpQuestions: How would you return only the k-th row using O(k) space?
How do values in Pascal's Triangle relate to combinations C(n, k)?

questions.name: Longest Consecutive Sequence
questions.description: Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence in O(n) time.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the longest chain of consecutive numbers in an unsorted array in O(n) time?
questions.hint: Store all numbers in a Hash Set. Only start counting a sequence if the current number is the sequence start (i.e., num - 1 is NOT in the set).
commonMistakes: Sorting the array first, which results in O(n log n) time complexity
Starting sequence checks from middle numbers, causing redundant work and failing linear time limits
followUpQuestions: How would you solve this using Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)?
What if the numbers arrive in a stream?

questions.name: Subarray Sum Equals K
questions.description: Given an array of integers nums and an integer k, return the total number of subarrays whose sum equals to k.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you count all contiguous subarrays summing to k when negative numbers are present?
questions.hint: Maintain a running prefix sum and a hash map storing frequency counts of past prefix sums. If (currentPrefixSum - k) exists in the map, add its frequency to your count.
commonMistakes: Assuming sliding window works when elements can be negative (sliding window fails with negative values)
Forgetting to initialize the hash map with {0: 1} to count subarrays starting from index 0
followUpQuestions: What if all elements are strictly non-negative—can you optimize to O(1) space?
How do you return the actual subarray indices instead of just the count?

questions.name: Valid Anagram
questions.description: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, and false otherwise.
questions.interviewQuestion: How can you verify whether two strings contain the exact same character frequencies?
questions.hint: Increment frequencies for characters in the first string and decrement for the second string using a fixed-size frequency array of 26 integers.
commonMistakes: Sorting both strings, which takes O(n log n) time instead of O(n)
Not checking if lengths are different right at the beginning
followUpQuestions: What if the inputs contain Unicode characters instead of lowercase ASCII?
How does string length impact space complexity choice?

questions.name: Group Anagrams
questions.description: Given an array of strings strs, group the anagrams together in any order.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you group an array of strings into sub-lists of anagrams efficiently?
questions.hint: Use a hash map where the key is either the sorted version of the string or its character frequency tuple, and the value is a list of matching strings.
commonMistakes: Comparing every string pair with every other string pair, resulting in O(N^2 * M) time
Using non-hashable collection types as hash map keys
followUpQuestions: How can you avoid string sorting to create the map key in O(N * M) time?
How would you handle massive data inputs that do not fit in memory?

questions.name: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
questions.description: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the maximum length of a substring with all distinct characters in linear time?
questions.hint: Use a sliding window with two pointers. Expand the right pointer to add characters, and shrink from the left pointer whenever a duplicate character is encountered.
commonMistakes: Shrinking the left pointer one by one instead of jumping directly to index + 1 using a map
Confusing 'substring' (contiguous) with 'subsequence' (non-contiguous)
followUpQuestions: What if you are allowed at most k duplicate characters in the window?
How would you optimize the solution for a small fixed character set?

questions.name: Longest Palindromic Substring
questions.description: Given a string s, return the longest palindromic substring in s.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you locate the longest contiguous palindrome within a string?
questions.hint: Iterate through each character (and pair of adjacent characters) treating them as centers, and expand outward as long as characters on both sides match.
commonMistakes: Only checking odd-length centers and forgetting even-length centers (e.g., 'abba')
Using a brute-force O(n^3) approach by checking every possible substring
followUpQuestions: How does Manacher's Algorithm solve this problem in linear O(n) time?
How would you count total palindromic substrings instead of finding the longest?

questions.name: Minimum Window Substring
questions.description: Given two strings s and t, return the minimum window substring of s such that every character in t (including duplicates) is included in the window.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the smallest substring containing all target characters in linear time?
questions.hint: Use two pointers for a sliding window. Expand the right edge until all target characters are covered, then contract the left edge to find the minimal valid window size.
commonMistakes: Checking the whole frequency map on every step instead of maintaining a 'satisfied characters' counter
Not handling duplicate target character requirements correctly
followUpQuestions: How would you modify this if order of target characters mattered?
What if you needed to find all starting indices of matching windows?

questions.name: Reverse Linked List
questions.description: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list, and return the reversed list.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you reverse a singly linked list in-place without using extra memory?
questions.hint: Maintain three pointers: previous, current, and next to flip the pointers iteratively.
questions.pattern: In-Place Reversal of a Linked List
commonMistakes: Losing reference to the next node before reassigning current.next
Returning the old head instead of the new head (prev)
Null pointer exceptions when checking current.next on empty lists
followUpQuestions: Can you solve it recursively as well as iteratively?
How would you reverse only a portion of the list between position m and n?

questions.name: Middle of the Linked List
questions.description: Given the head of a singly linked list, return the middle node of the linked list. If there are two middle nodes, return the second middle node.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the middle node of a linked list in a single pass?
questions.hint: Use the Fast & Slow pointer approach (Floyd's Tortoise and Hare algorithm).
commonMistakes: Not checking if fast or fast.next is null in the loop condition
Incorrectly returning the first middle node when the list length is even
followUpQuestions: What if you need to return the first middle node instead of the second for even-length lists?
How would you adapt this to find the node at one-third of the list length?

questions.name: Merge Two Sorted Lists
questions.description: You are given the heads of two sorted linked lists list1 and list2. Merge the two lists into one sorted list by splicing together the nodes of the first two lists.
questions.interviewQuestion: How can you merge two sorted linked lists into a single sorted list efficiently?
questions.hint: Use a dummy node to easily construct the new merged list pointer sequence.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to attach the remaining nodes after one list becomes empty
Not creating a dummy node, leading to tedious edge-case logic for the head node
followUpQuestions: How would you merge K sorted linked lists?
Can you implement this solution recursively?

questions.name: Linked List Cycle
questions.description: Given head, the head of a linked list, determine if the linked list has a cycle in it.
questions.interviewQuestion: How can you detect if a linked list contains a cycle without modifying the structure or using extra space?
questions.hint: If a fast pointer moves two steps and a slow pointer moves one step, they will eventually meet if a cycle exists.
commonMistakes: Not checking for null pointers on fast and fast.next before dereferencing
Comparing node values instead of node object references
followUpQuestions: How would you determine the length of the cycle?
What is the mathematical proof that fast and slow pointers will meet if a cycle exists?

questions.name: Linked List Cycle II
questions.description: Given the head of a linked list, return the node where the cycle begins. If there is no cycle, return null.
questions.interviewQuestion: Once a cycle is detected using Floyd's algorithm, how do you locate the exact node where the cycle starts?
questions.hint: Reset one pointer to head and move both pointers one step at a time; they will meet at the cycle entry node.
commonMistakes: Assuming the meeting point of fast and slow pointers is the start of the cycle
Failing to handle lists without cycles properly
followUpQuestions: Why does moving one pointer to the head and running both at speed 1 guarantee meeting at the entry node?
Can this pattern be applied to find a duplicate number in an array?

questions.name: Remove Nth Node From End of List
questions.description: Given the head of a linked list, remove the nth node from the end of the list and return its head.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you remove the Nth node from the end of a linked list in a single traversal pass?
questions.hint: Advance a fast pointer by N+1 steps first, then move fast and slow pointers together.
commonMistakes: Off-by-one errors when advancing the fast pointer initially
Not using a dummy node, which makes removing the head node an edge case
followUpQuestions: How would you handle cases where N is greater than the length of the list?
Could you solve this using recursion?

questions.name: Palindrome Linked List
questions.description: Given the head of a singly linked list, return true if it is a palindrome or false otherwise.
questions.interviewQuestion: How can you check if a singly linked list is a palindrome in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space?
questions.hint: Find the middle, reverse the second half of the list, and compare values node by node.
commonMistakes: Not properly handling odd vs. even length lists
Forgetting to restore the modified list back to its original state (if required by constraints)
followUpQuestions: Can you restore the list back to its original structure before returning?
How would you check this using recursion and an external pointer?

questions.name: Intersection of Two Linked Lists
questions.description: Given the heads of two singly linked-lists headA and headB, return the node at which the two lists intersect. If the two linked lists have no intersection, return null.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the intersection node of two singly linked lists without calculating their exact lengths explicitly?
questions.hint: Traverse list A then list B, and vice versa; two pointers will align at the intersection due to equal total distance.
commonMistakes: Comparing node values instead of node memory references
Infinite loop if pointer redirection at null is handled incorrectly
followUpQuestions: How would you solve this by counting lengths first?
What if one or both lists contain cycles?

questions.name: Add Two Numbers
questions.description: You are given two non-empty linked lists representing two non-negative integers. The digits are stored in reverse order. Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you add two numbers represented as linked lists stored in reverse order?
questions.hint: Simulate elementary addition node-by-node, keeping track of carry.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to append the final carry node after exiting the loop
Not handling lists of unequal lengths properly
followUpQuestions: What if the digits are stored in most-significant-digit-first (forward) order?
How would you handle arbitrarily large numbers?

questions.name: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
questions.description: Given the head of a linked list, reverse the nodes of a list k at a time, and return the modified list. If the number of nodes is not a multiple of k then left-out nodes at the end should remain as they are.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you reverse nodes of a linked list in chunks of k, keeping remaining nodes unchanged if less than k remain?
questions.hint: Count k nodes first; if present, reverse them and recursively process the remaining sublist.
commonMistakes: Reversing trailing nodes even when they are fewer than k
Losing pointers between reversed sub-groups
followUpQuestions: Can you solve this iteratively in O(1) extra memory space?
What if remaining nodes (< k) should also be reversed?

questions.name: Copy List with Random Pointer
questions.description: Construct a deep copy of a linked list where each node contains an additional random pointer which could point to any node in the list or null.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you perform a deep copy of a linked list with random pointers in O(1) space?
questions.hint: Interleave cloned nodes between original nodes to preserve reference mapping without extra memory.
commonMistakes: Shallow copying random pointers instead of pointing to newly cloned nodes
Failing to detach the interleaved lists properly at the end
followUpQuestions: How can you solve this using a Hash Map first, and what are its trade-offs?
How would you clone a general graph structure with arbitrary pointers?

questions.name: Sort List
questions.description: Given the head of a linked list, return the list after sorting it in ascending order using O(n log n) time and O(1) space complexity.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you sort a linked list in O(n log n) time complexity?
questions.hint: Use Merge Sort: split the list into halves using fast/slow pointers, sort each half, and merge them.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to sever the link (mid.next = null) when splitting the list
Stack overflow when using recursion on very large lists without base cases
followUpQuestions: How would you implement bottom-up Merge Sort to guarantee true O(1) space complexity?
Why is Quick Sort less ideal than Merge Sort for singly linked lists?

questions.name: Odd Even Linked List
questions.description: Given the head of a singly linked list, group all the nodes with odd indices together followed by the nodes with even indices, and return the reordered list.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you rearrange a linked list to group odd-indexed nodes before even-indexed nodes in O(1) space?
questions.hint: Maintain separate odd and even pointers, weave them through the list, and attach evenHead at the end of odd.
commonMistakes: Confusing node values with node indices (1-indexed position)
Creating cyclic references at the tail of the even list
followUpQuestions: How would you adapt this to group nodes by value (even vs. odd value) instead of index?
What if you need to partition the list into three groups?

questions.name: Rotate List
questions.description: Given the head of a linked list, rotate the list to the right by k places.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you rotate a linked list right by K positions efficiently?
questions.hint: Connect the tail to the head to form a ring, then find the new tail at position (length - k % length) and break the ring.
commonMistakes: Not taking k % length when k is much larger than the list size
Null pointer errors on empty or single-element lists
followUpQuestions: How would you rotate the list to the left instead of right?
What if k is negative?

questions.name: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List
questions.description: Given a doubly linked list where nodes may have a child pointer pointing to a separate doubly linked list, flatten the list so that all the nodes appear in a single-level, doubly linked list.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you flatten a multi-level doubly linked list into a single level depth-first order?
questions.hint: Traverse nodes sequentially; when a child is found, insert child sub-chain between current and current.next.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to set current.child to null after stitching
Failing to maintain the correct prev pointers when inserting child sublists
followUpQuestions: Can you solve this iteratively using an explicit Stack?
How would you flatten the list breadth-first (BFS) instead of depth-first?

questions.name: Valid Parentheses
questions.description: Given a string s containing just the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine if the input string is valid.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you check if a string with nested brackets is balanced using a stack?
questions.hint: Push opening brackets onto a stack; when a closing bracket is seen, check if it matches the stack's top element.
commonMistakes: Popping from an empty stack when encountering an extra closing bracket
Forgetting to check if the stack is completely empty at the end of traversal
followUpQuestions: How would you handle wildcard characters like '*' that can act as any bracket?
What if the string contains non-bracket characters interspersed throughout?

questions.name: Min Stack
questions.description: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element in constant time.
questions.interviewQuestion: How can you design a stack where retrieving the minimum element takes O(1) time complexity?
questions.hint: Store each value alongside the current minimum value at that point in the stack, or maintain a secondary stack of minimums.
commonMistakes: Attempting to iterate through the stack to find the minimum in O(n) instead of O(1)
Not correctly updating or popping the auxiliary minimum stack when elements are removed
followUpQuestions: Can you implement a Min Stack with O(1) space complexity on average using math tricks?
How would you implement a Max Stack with similar requirements?

questions.name: Implement Queue using Stacks
questions.description: Implement a first-in-first-out (FIFO) queue using only two stacks. The implemented queue should support push, peek, pop, and empty operations.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you emulate FIFO queue behavior using two LIFO stacks with amortized O(1) operations?
questions.hint: Use one stack for incoming elements (push) and another for outgoing elements (pop/peek). Transfer elements only when the outgoing stack is empty.
commonMistakes: Shuffling elements back and forth between stacks on every single operation instead of lazily on pop/peek
Forgetting to check if the output stack is empty before popping
followUpQuestions: Why is the amortized time complexity of pop() equal to O(1)?
Can you design this where push is O(1) and pop is worst-case O(1) without amortized delays?

questions.name: Implement Stack using Queues
questions.description: Implement a last-in-first-out (LIFO) stack using only queues. The implemented stack should support push, top, pop, and empty operations.
questions.interviewQuestion: How can you implement LIFO stack behavior using standard FIFO queues?
questions.hint: When pushing a new element, enqueue it and rotate the preceding elements to the back of the queue.
commonMistakes: Rotating the queue an incorrect number of times during push
Confusing queue front and rear operations
followUpQuestions: Can you implement this using only a single queue instead of two?
What are the trade-offs between making push O(n) versus pop O(n)?

questions.name: Daily Temperatures
questions.description: Given an array of integers temperatures represents the daily temperatures, return an array answer such that answer[i] is the number of days you have to wait after the i-th day to get a warmer temperature.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the next larger element distance for every element in an array efficiently?
questions.hint: Use a monotonic decreasing stack to store element indices. Resolve elements when a warmer temperature is encountered.
commonMistakes: Storing temperature values in the stack instead of indices
Using a nested loop resulting in O(n²) time complexity
followUpQuestions: How would you modify the solution if temperatures were given as a stream?
What if you needed to find the previous warmer day instead of the next?

questions.name: Next Greater Element I
questions.description: The next greater element of some element x in an array is the first greater element that is to the right of x in the same array. Return an array answer corresponding to queries in nums1 relative to nums2.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you precompute the next greater element for all items in an array using a Monotonic Stack?
questions.hint: Traverse nums2 with a monotonic stack and map each element to its next greater element in a Hash Map.
commonMistakes: Re-searching nums2 for every element in nums1 individually
Not handling elements that have no next greater element (default to -1)
followUpQuestions: How does the solution change if nums2 contains duplicate values?
Can this be solved by processing the array from right to left?

questions.name: Next Greater Element II
questions.description: Given a circular integer array nums, return the next greater number for every element in nums.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the next greater element in a circular array?
questions.hint: Simulate a circular array by traversing the array twice (length 2 * n) using index modulo (i % n) with a monotonic stack.
commonMistakes: Pushing elements to the stack during the second pass, causing duplicates
Actually duplicating the array memory instead of using modulo indexing
followUpQuestions: Can you solve this starting from right to left instead of left to right?
What is the maximum number of times any index will be pushed/popped from the stack?

questions.name: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
questions.description: Given an array of integers heights representing the histogram's bar height where the width of each bar is 1, return the area of the largest rectangle in the histogram.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you calculate the maximum rectangular area in a histogram in O(n) time?
questions.hint: Use a monotonic increasing stack of indices. When a shorter bar is found, pop the stack and calculate the area with the popped height as the bottleneck.
commonMistakes: Incorrectly calculating width when the stack becomes empty after popping
Forgetting to flush remaining items in the stack at the end of traversal
followUpQuestions: How would you extend this to find the maximal rectangle in a 2D binary matrix?
Can this problem be solved using Divide and Conquer?

questions.name: Asteroid Collision
questions.description: We are given an array asteroids of integers representing asteroids in a row. Find out the state of the asteroids after all collisions.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you simulate collisions between moving objects traveling in opposite directions using a stack?
questions.hint: Collisions only occur when top of stack moves right (> 0) and current asteroid moves left (< 0). Use a stack to resolve collisions sequentially.
commonMistakes: Assuming collisions occur when stack top moves left (< 0) and current moves right (> 0)
Not handling equal-sized colliding asteroids properly (both explode)
followUpQuestions: What if asteroids move at different speeds instead of uniform speed?
Can you implement this in-place without using an explicit stack array?

questions.name: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
questions.description: Evaluate the value of an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation (Postfix). Valid operators are '+', '-', '*', and '/'.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you evaluate postfix expressions using a stack?
questions.hint: Push numbers onto the stack. When an operator is encountered, pop the top two numbers, evaluate, and push the result back.
commonMistakes: Reversing the operand order during subtraction and division (e.g., performing b / a instead of a / b)
Failing to handle integer truncation toward zero for negative division
followUpQuestions: How would you evaluate Infix notation directly (Shunting Yard algorithm)?
How would you handle custom unary operators?

questions.name: Decode String
questions.description: Given an encoded string, return its decoded string. The encoding rule is: k[encoded_string], where the encoded_string inside the square brackets is being repeated exactly k times.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you expand nested string repetitions like '3[a2[c]]' using a stack?
questions.hint: Maintain two stacks or a stack of pairs for numbers and prefix strings. Push current state on '[' and pop/repeat on ']'.
commonMistakes: Not parsing multi-digit numbers correctly (e.g. '10[a]')
Incorrect string concatenation order when popping from the stack
followUpQuestions: Can you solve this recursively using Depth-First Search?
How would you handle malformed or unbalanced bracket inputs?

questions.name: Basic Calculator
questions.description: Given a string s representing a valid expression, implement a basic calculator to evaluate it. s consists of digits, '+', '-', '(', ')', and spaces.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you evaluate mathematical expressions containing parentheses, plus, and minus signs?
questions.hint: Track sign and running sum. Push running sum and current sign to stack upon reaching '(', and pop to combine results upon reaching ')'.
commonMistakes: Mismanaging unary minus signs at the start or immediately after opening parentheses
Incorrect sign distribution across nested parentheses
followUpQuestions: How would you extend this to support multiplication '*' and division '/' (Basic Calculator II)?
How do you build an Expression Tree from this input?

questions.name: Remove K Digits
questions.description: Given string num representing a non-negative integer, and an integer k, return the smallest possible integer after removing k digits from num.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you construct the smallest number by removing K digits using a greedy approach with a monotonic stack?
questions.hint: Use a monotonic increasing stack to ensure earlier digits are as small as possible. Pop whenever stack top is greater than current digit.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to pop remaining digits if K is still greater than 0 after parsing all digits
Leaving leading zeros in the final formatted string output
followUpQuestions: What if you need to create the largest number instead of the smallest?
How does the problem change if relative order doesn't need to be preserved?

questions.name: Online Stock Span
questions.description: Design an algorithm that collects daily price quotes for some stock and returns the span of that stock's price for the current day (consecutive days price <= current).
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you design a streaming data structure to compute stock price spans efficiently?
questions.hint: Store pairs of [price, span] in a monotonic decreasing stack and accumulate spans of smaller prices.
commonMistakes: Re-iterating past historical prices on every call to next(), leading to O(n) per call instead of O(1) amortized
Not accumulating spans recursively/combining them when popping elements
followUpQuestions: What is the amortized time complexity of each call to next()?
How would you clear older memory if only a sliding time window matters?

questions.name: Sliding Window Maximum
questions.description: You are given an array of integers nums and a sliding window of size k moving from left to right. Return the max sliding window.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the maximum element in every sliding window of size K in O(n) time?
questions.hint: Use a Monotonic Deque (Double-ended Queue) storing indices, keeping elements in decreasing order.
commonMistakes: Storing values instead of indices in the deque, making it hard to check if elements have fallen out of the window
Failing to clean up smaller values from the back of the deque before adding new elements
followUpQuestions: Can you solve this using a Max-Heap, and what would the time complexity be?
How can this be solved using dynamic programming with prefix/suffix max arrays?

questions.name: Contains Duplicate
questions.description: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice in the array, and return false if every element is distinct.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you check if an array contains duplicate elements in O(n) time?
questions.hint: Iterate through the array while storing seen elements in a Hash Set to check for duplicates in O(1) time.
commonMistakes: Using a nested loop resulting in O(n²) time complexity
Sorting the array first, which increases time complexity to O(n log n)
followUpQuestions: How would you solve this if you are constrained to O(1) extra space?
What if duplicate elements must appear within k distance of each other (Contains Duplicate II)?

questions.name: Two Sum
questions.description: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target.
questions.interviewQuestion: How can you find two numbers in an array that add up to a target in single pass O(n) time?
questions.hint: For each number, check if target - num exists in a Hash Map. If not, insert current number and its index into the map.
commonMistakes: Using the same element twice
Checking all pairs with nested loops resulting in O(n²) complexity
followUpQuestions: What if the array is sorted?
What if all unique pairs are required instead of just indices?
What if numbers arrive continuously as a stream?

questions.name: Valid Anagram
questions.description: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, and false otherwise.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you verify if two strings are anagrams in O(n) time using O(1) auxiliary space for English alphabet characters?
questions.hint: Use a fixed-size frequency array of length 26 to count character occurrences across both strings.
commonMistakes: Not checking if lengths of both strings are equal before iterating
Sorting both strings, which takes O(n log n) time
followUpQuestions: What if the inputs contain Unicode characters instead of lower-case ASCII?
How would you adapt this if space complexity must strictly be O(1) regardless of alphabet size?

questions.name: Group Anagrams
questions.description: Given an array of strings strs, group the anagrams together. You can return the answer in any order.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you group a list of strings by their anagram frequency signature?
questions.hint: Use either a sorted version of each string or a character count tuple as a Hash Map key to group strings.
commonMistakes: Using an unhashable type (like a raw array/list) as a Hash Map key without serializing it
Relying on string sorting when character count encoding could be faster for very long strings
followUpQuestions: What is the trade-off between using sorted string keys vs. character frequency tuple keys?
How would you optimize this if strings contain full Unicode characters?

questions.name: Top K Frequent Elements
questions.description: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the top K most frequent elements in an array in O(n) linear time?
questions.hint: Count frequencies using a Hash Map, then use Bucket Sort where array indices represent element frequencies.
commonMistakes: Sorting the frequency entries directly, resulting in O(n log n) complexity
Index out-of-bounds error on the bucket array (needs size n + 1)
followUpQuestions: How would you solve this using a Min-Heap, and what would be the time complexity?
Can this be solved using the QuickSelect algorithm?

questions.name: Longest Consecutive Sequence
questions.description: Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the longest sequence of consecutive integers in an unsorted array in linear O(n) time?
questions.hint: Insert numbers into a Set. Only start counting a sequence from numbers where (num - 1) is NOT in the set.
commonMistakes: Checking sequences starting at every number, leading to O(n²) worst-case execution
Sorting the array first, violating the strict O(n) runtime constraint
followUpQuestions: Why does checking `(num - 1) not in set` guarantee overall O(n) linear complexity?
How would you return the actual consecutive numbers instead of just the sequence length?

questions.name: Subarray Sum Equals K
questions.description: Given an array of integers nums and an integer k, return the total number of subarrays whose sum equals to k.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the total number of contiguous subarrays that sum to K in O(n) time?
questions.hint: Use a Prefix Sum coupled with a Hash Map storing frequencies of observed prefix sums.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to initialize the prefix sum map with `{0: 1}` to account for subarrays starting at index 0
Assuming sliding window works when negative numbers exist in the array
followUpQuestions: Why doesn't a standard two-pointer sliding window work if the array contains negative numbers?
How would you adapt this to return the shortest continuous subarray with sum equal to k?

questions.name: Ransom Note
questions.description: Given two strings ransomNote and magazine, return true if ransomNote can be constructed by using the letters from magazine and false otherwise.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you check if a target string can be formed from available letter frequencies in another string?
questions.hint: Count character frequencies in magazine and decrement counts for each letter in ransomNote.
commonMistakes: Re-counting character frequencies in magazine multiple times
Assuming each letter in magazine can be reused indefinitely
followUpQuestions: What if magazine is updated dynamically in real-time streaming?
How does space complexity change if full Unicode characters are supported?

questions.name: Isomorphic Strings
questions.description: Given two strings s and t, determine if they are isomorphic. Two strings s and t are isomorphic if the characters in s can be replaced to get t.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you verify if two strings have a valid 1-to-1 character mapping in both directions?
questions.hint: Use two Hash Maps (or last-seen index maps) to build bidirectional mapping between characters of s and t.
commonMistakes: Only checking mapping in one direction (s -> t) and missing many-to-one mapping violations (t -> s)
Confusing string length validation with character mapping logic
followUpQuestions: Can you solve this using a single map that tracks last-seen index positions for both strings?
How would you handle sentence-level isomorphic checking (Word Pattern)?

questions.name: Happy Number
questions.description: Write an algorithm to determine if a number n is happy. A happy number is defined by replacing the number by the sum of the squares of its digits until it equals 1 or loops indefinitely.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you detect infinite cycles when repeatedly replacing a number by the sum of its squared digits?
questions.hint: Track previously seen sum values in a Hash Set, or use Floyd's Fast & Slow pointers cycle detection.
questions.pattern: Hash Set Cycle Detection / Fast & Slow Pointers
prerequisites: Hash Sets or Fast & Slow Pointers
commonMistakes: Infinite loop caused by not tracking previously generated numbers
Incorrect digit extraction logic (modulo and integer division)
followUpQuestions: Can you solve this problem with O(1) auxiliary space without using a Hash Set?
What is the mathematical proof that numbers will either reach 1 or cycle in a small bounded range?

questions.name: Find All Anagrams in a String
questions.description: Given two strings s and p, return an array of all the start indices of p's anagrams in s. You may return the answer in any order.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find all starting indices of a target string's anagrams within a larger text string?
questions.hint: Maintain a fixed-size sliding window of length p.length and compare frequency maps as the window moves.
commonMistakes: Recomputing character counts for the entire window from scratch at each step (O(n * m))
Not removing zero-count elements from frequency maps when comparing hash maps
followUpQuestions: How can you optimize match comparison from O(26) to O(1) using a `matches` counter variable?
What if string s is too large to fit in memory?

questions.name: Word Pattern
questions.description: Given a pattern and a string s, find if s follows the same pattern. Here follow means a full match, such that there is a bijection between a letter in pattern and a non-empty word in s.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you establish a bijection between characters in a pattern and space-delimited words in a string?
questions.hint: Split s into words and maintain dual mappings: character-to-word and word-to-character.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to verify if pattern length equals the total number of words in s
Mapping multiple pattern characters to the same word
followUpQuestions: Can you solve this without explicitly allocating memory for the split words array?
How would you extend this pattern matching to handle multi-character symbols in the pattern?

questions.name: 4Sum II
questions.description: Given four integer arrays nums1, nums2, nums3, and nums4 all of length n, return the number of tuples (i, j, k, l) such that nums1[i] + nums2[j] + nums3[k] + nums4[l] == 0.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you count quadruplets across four separate arrays that sum to zero in O(n²) time?
questions.hint: Store sums of all pairs from array A and B in a Hash Map, then iterate through pairs of C and D checking for `- (c + d)`.
commonMistakes: Trying brute-force with 4 nested loops resulting in O(n⁴) execution time
Splitting into 3 arrays vs 1 array instead of balanced 2 arrays vs 2 arrays grouping
followUpQuestions: How would this approach extend to KSum across K different arrays?
What are the space-time trade-offs between grouping (3 vs 1) versus (2 vs 2)?

questions.name: First Unique Character in a String
questions.description: Given a string s, find the first non-repeating character in it and return its index. If it does not exist, return -1.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the first non-repeating character in a string in two passes?
questions.hint: Build a frequency map in the first pass, then iterate through string indices to find the first character with count 1.
commonMistakes: Iterating over frequency map keys instead of original string indices during the second pass
Using nested string searches like indexOf/lastIndexOf inside a loop leading to O(n²)
followUpQuestions: How would you find the first unique character in a continuous real-time data stream?
Can this be solved in a single pass using a Queue alongside a Hash Map?

questions.name: Design HashMap
questions.description: Design a HashMap without using any built-in hash table libraries. Implement put, get, and remove methods.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you implement a Hash Map from scratch handling collision resolution?
questions.hint: Use an array of buckets combined with linked lists or key-value pair lists to handle collisions via Separate Chaining.
commonMistakes: Using a small prime modulus causing excessive chain collisions
Failing to properly update existing key values when calling `put()`
followUpQuestions: How would you implement dynamic resizing (rehashing) when load factor exceeds a threshold?
What are the trade-offs between Separate Chaining and Open Addressing (Linear Probing)?

questions.name: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
questions.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the maximum depth or height of a binary tree using recursion?
questions.hint: The height of a tree is 1 plus the maximum depth of its left and right subtrees.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the base case for empty nodes (returning 0)
Counting nodes instead of edges (depending on standard height definition)
followUpQuestions: How would you solve this iteratively using Breadth-First Search (BFS)?
What is the difference between maximum depth and minimum depth?

questions.name: Same Tree
questions.description: Given the roots of two binary trees p and q, write a function to check if they are the same or not.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you determine if two binary trees are structurally identical with matching node values?
questions.hint: Check if both nodes are null, if one is null, and if their values match. Recursively verify left and right subtrees.
commonMistakes: Not handling cases where one tree node is null while the other is not
Short-circuiting value evaluation before checking for null pointers
followUpQuestions: How would you solve this problem iteratively using a Queue or Stack?
How does this relate to tree serialization?

questions.name: Symmetric Tree
questions.description: Given the root of a binary tree, check whether it is a mirror of itself (i.e., symmetric around its center).
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you check if a binary tree is symmetric around its root?
questions.hint: Write a helper function that takes two nodes and checks if `t1.left` mirrors `t2.right` and `t1.right` mirrors `t2.left`.
commonMistakes: Comparing left and right children of the same node instead of cross-comparing subtrees
Incorrectly returning true when only tree structure matches but values differ
followUpQuestions: Can you implement this iteratively using a Queue?
How does subtree symmetry change if values can be duplicated?

questions.name: Binary Tree Inorder Traversal
questions.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the inorder traversal of its nodes' values.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you perform an inorder traversal (Left-Root-Right) iteratively without recursion?
questions.hint: Use an explicit Stack. Traverse all the way to the leftmost node first, popping and moving right.
commonMistakes: Popping nodes from the stack before completely traversing down the left subtree
Infinite loops by revisiting processed left children
followUpQuestions: Can you perform an Inorder Traversal with O(1) space complexity (Morris Traversal)?
What property does an inorder traversal guarantee on a Binary Search Tree (BST)?

questions.name: Binary Tree Preorder Traversal
questions.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the preorder traversal of its nodes' values.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you perform a preorder traversal (Root-Left-Right) using an iterative stack approach?
questions.hint: Push root to stack. When popping a node, process it, then push right child first, then left child.
commonMistakes: Pushing the left child to stack before the right child (causes right-first processing order)
Not checking for null children before pushing to the stack
followUpQuestions: How would you serialize a tree using Preorder Traversal?
Can you convert an iterative Preorder Traversal to Morris Traversal?

questions.name: Binary Tree Postorder Traversal
questions.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the postorder traversal of its nodes' values.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you implement an iterative postorder traversal (Left-Right-Root)?
questions.hint: Perform a modified preorder traversal (Root-Right-Left) using a stack, then reverse the final output list.
commonMistakes: Complex single-stack implementations getting stuck in infinite loops revisiting right nodes
Confusing postorder with reverse inorder traversal
followUpQuestions: How can you implement true single-stack Postorder Traversal without reversing the result?
Why is Postorder Traversal useful for bottom-up calculation problems like tree deletion?

questions.name: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
questions.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the level order traversal of its nodes' values. (i.e., from left to right, level by level).
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you perform a Breadth-First Search (BFS) level-by-level traversal on a binary tree?
questions.hint: Use a FIFO Queue and process nodes level by level using the snapshot size of the queue at each level step.
commonMistakes: Not capturing `queue.length` at the start of each level loop iteration
Using a stack instead of a queue, causing depth-first ordering
followUpQuestions: How would you modify this to output levels in bottom-up order?
Can you solve this using DFS by passing the current level depth as a parameter?

questions.name: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
questions.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the zigzag level order traversal of its nodes' values. (i.e., from left to right, then right to left for the next level and alternate between).
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you perform a level order traversal that alternates direction every level?
questions.hint: Use standard BFS queue level order traversal, but flip a boolean flag to append level elements backwards or forward.
commonMistakes: Reversing child insertion order in the queue instead of value insertion order in level arrays
Forgetting to toggle the direction flag after finishing each level
followUpQuestions: How can you implement this using two Stacks instead of a Queue?
What is the memory trade-off between using a Deque vs flipping arrays?

questions.name: Diameter of Binary Tree
questions.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the length of the diameter of the tree. The diameter of a binary tree is the length of the longest path between any two nodes in a tree.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you calculate the longest path between any two nodes in a binary tree?
questions.hint: At each node, the longest path passing through it is `leftHeight + rightHeight`. Compute height recursively while updating a global max.
commonMistakes: Assuming the diameter path must pass through the root node of the entire tree
Returning path length in terms of node count instead of edge count
followUpQuestions: How would you return the actual node path corresponding to the diameter?
How does this problem adapt to General N-ary Trees?

questions.name: Balanced Binary Tree
questions.description: Given a binary tree, determine if it is height-balanced (a binary tree in which the left and right subtrees of every node differ in height by no more than 1).
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you check if a binary tree is height-balanced in O(n) time complexity?
questions.hint: Return `-1` from bottom-up height computation if a subtree is unbalanced to short-circuit calculation.
commonMistakes: Calculating height at every single node separately, resulting in O(n²) top-down time complexity
Forgetting to check balance condition on subtrees before parent nodes
followUpQuestions: Why is bottom-up DFS preferable over top-down recursion for this problem?
How does tree balance impact operations on Binary Search Trees?

questions.name: Path Sum
questions.description: Given the root of a binary tree and an integer targetSum, return true if the tree has a root-to-leaf path such that adding up all the values along the path equals targetSum.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you check if a root-to-leaf path exists with a given sum?
questions.hint: Subtract node value from targetSum recursively and check if remaining sum equals target at a leaf node.
commonMistakes: Checking the sum condition on a non-leaf node
Not handling negative node values properly
followUpQuestions: How would you collect all matching root-to-leaf paths (Path Sum II)?
What if paths do not need to start at root or end at a leaf (Path Sum III)?

questions.name: Binary Tree Right Side View
questions.description: Given the root of a binary tree, imagine yourself standing on the right side of it, return the values of the nodes you can see ordered from top to bottom.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the rightmost visible node at each level of a binary tree?
questions.hint: Perform level order BFS and take the last element of each level, or perform DFS prioritizing Right child first.
commonMistakes: Assuming the right view consists only of nodes on the right spine of the tree
Forgetting left nodes that are deeper than any right subtrees
followUpQuestions: How would you modify this algorithm for the Left Side View?
How would you track the Top View or Bottom View of a tree?

questions.name: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
questions.description: Given a binary tree, find the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of two given nodes in the tree.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the lowest common ancestor of two target nodes in a general binary tree?
questions.hint: Recurse left and right. If both return non-null, current node is the LCA. Otherwise return whichever is non-null.
commonMistakes: Confusing general binary tree LCA with BST LCA logic
Assuming target nodes p and q might not exist in the tree when stated otherwise
followUpQuestions: How would you solve LCA if nodes have parent pointers?
How would this change if one or both target nodes might not exist in the tree?

questions.name: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
questions.description: Given two integer arrays preorder and inorder where preorder is the preorder traversal of a binary tree and inorder is the inorder traversal of the same tree, construct and return the binary tree.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you reconstruct a unique binary tree from its preorder and inorder traversals?
questions.hint: The first element of preorder is root. Locate this root in inorder array to divide into left and right subtrees.
questions.pattern: Divide and Conquer / Hash Map Indexing
commonMistakes: Searching for root index linearly in inorder array instead of precomputing indices using a Hash Map
Off-by-one errors in index slicing bounds
followUpQuestions: Can you reconstruct a tree from Inorder and Postorder traversals?
Why is it impossible to reconstruct a unique tree using only Preorder and Postorder without strict full binary tree guarantees?

questions.name: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List
questions.description: Given the root of a binary tree, flatten the tree into a 'linked list' in-place matching the preorder traversal order.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you flatten a binary tree into a right-skewed linked list in-place matching preorder sequence?
questions.hint: For each node with a left child, find the rightmost node of left subtree, attach `current.right` there, and move left subtree to right.
questions.pattern: Morris Traversal Pointer Stitching / Reverse Postorder DFS
commonMistakes: Forgetting to nullify `current.left` after reassigning it to `current.right`
Losing track of right subtrees during traversal
followUpQuestions: How can you solve this using a reverse postorder recursive approach (Right-Left-Root)?
Can this be performed using an explicit Stack?

questions.name: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
questions.description: Design an algorithm to serialize a binary tree to a string and deserialize a string back to the original binary tree structure.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you serialize and deserialize a binary tree structure cleanly?
questions.hint: Use preorder DFS traversal including 'null' markers for missing children, and rebuild recursively using a queue/pointer.
commonMistakes: Omitting null markers, which makes deserialization ambiguous for trees with duplicate values
Using inefficient string concatenation during serialization instead of join
followUpQuestions: How would you implement level-order (BFS) serialization instead of DFS?
How can you optimize string output size for minimal network bandwidth?

questions.name: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
questions.description: A path in a binary tree is a sequence of nodes where each pair of adjacent nodes has an edge connecting them. Return the maximum path sum of any non-empty path.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the maximum path sum across any path in a binary tree?
questions.hint: At each node, calculate max gain from left and right subtrees (clamp negative gains to 0). Path sum through node is `node.val + leftGain + rightGain`.
commonMistakes: Including negative child branch gains in parent path calculation instead of capping at 0
Returning path sums that branch in both directions to parent calls
followUpQuestions: How do you return the sequence of nodes forming the max path sum?
How does this problem simplify if node values are guaranteed to be non-negative?

questions.name: Count Complete Tree Nodes
questions.description: Given the root of a complete binary tree, return the number of the nodes in the tree in less than O(n) time complexity.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you count nodes in a complete binary tree in sub-linear O((log n)²) time?
questions.hint: Compare left and right subtree heights. If equal, left subtree is a perfect tree; otherwise right subtree is perfect.
questions.pattern: Binary Search on Complete Binary Trees
commonMistakes: Using standard DFS counting, taking O(n) time and ignoring tree completeness
Calculating height across all subtrees repeatedly without leveraging complete tree height logic
followUpQuestions: Can you solve this using pure Binary Search on leaf nodes?
What is the total number of nodes in a perfect binary tree of height h?

questions.name: Invert Binary Tree
questions.description: Given the root of a binary tree, invert the tree, and return its root.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you invert or create a mirror image of a binary tree?
questions.hint: Recursively swap left and right subtrees for every node in the tree.
commonMistakes: Swapping subtree nodes before storing temporary references
Forgetting base null check condition
followUpQuestions: Can you solve this iteratively using a Queue or Stack?
How does inverting a tree affect its Inorder Traversal order?

questions.name: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
questions.description: Given the root of a binary search tree (BST) and an integer k, return the kth smallest value (1-indexed) of all the values of the nodes in the tree.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the Kth smallest element in a Binary Search Tree (BST)?
questions.hint: Perform iterative Inorder Traversal; the Kth node popped/visited in order is the result.
commonMistakes: Traversing entire tree into an array first when early termination at K items is possible
Confusing BST properties with general binary tree ordering
followUpQuestions: If the BST is modified frequently (insert/delete) and you need to query Kth smallest often, how would you optimize it?
How would you find the Kth largest element instead?

questions.name: Kth Largest Element in an Array
questions.description: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth largest element in the array.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the Kth largest element in an unsorted array efficiently without fully sorting it?
questions.hint: Maintain a Min-Heap of size K. Iterate through the array; if the current element is larger than the top of the heap, pop the top and insert the current element.
commonMistakes: Using a Max-Heap of size N instead of a Min-Heap of size K, which takes O(n log n) space and time
Confusing 0-indexed positions with Kth largest rank
followUpQuestions: Can you solve this in O(n) average time complexity using QuickSelect?
How would you handle finding the Kth largest element in a continuous data stream?

questions.name: Top K Frequent Elements
questions.description: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you extract the K most frequent items from an array using a Priority Queue?
questions.hint: Count frequencies using a Hash Map, then maintain a Min-Heap of size K based on frequency.
commonMistakes: Storing elements in a Max-Heap without limiting heap size to K
Sorting all unique elements by frequency, leading to O(u log u) complexity where u is unique count
followUpQuestions: How can you solve this in O(n) linear time using Bucket Sort?
How would you handle a tie in frequency between elements?

questions.name: K Closest Points to Origin
questions.description: Given an array of points where points[i] = [xi, yi] represents a point on the X-Y plane and an integer k, return the k closest points to the origin (0, 0).
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you find the K points closest to the origin on a 2D plane?
questions.hint: Maintain a Max-Heap of size K storing points ordered by Euclidean distance squared to avoid floating-point operations.
commonMistakes: Calculating actual square roots for distances instead of comparing squared distances ($x^2 + y^2$)
Using a Min-Heap of size N, which takes O(n log n) time instead of O(n log k)
followUpQuestions: Can this be optimized to O(n) average time using QuickSelect?
How would you scale this solution if point data is distributed across multiple machines?

questions.name: Find Median from Data Stream
questions.description: Implement the MedianFinder class to support adding numbers from a data stream and finding the median of current numbers in O(1) time.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you maintain the running median of a continuously streaming sequence of numbers?
questions.hint: Use two heaps: a Max-Heap for the smaller half of numbers and a Min-Heap for the larger half, keeping their sizes balanced within 1.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to rebalance the two heaps after pushing new elements
Casting integer division incorrectly when calculating the mean of two middle numbers
followUpQuestions: What if 99% of all integer numbers in the stream are between 0 and 100?
How would you remove numbers or support a sliding window median?
questions.timeComplexity: O(log n) for addNum, O(1) for findMedian

questions.name: Merge k Sorted Lists
questions.description: You are given an array of k linked-lists lists, each linked-list is sorted in ascending order. Merge all the linked-lists into one sorted linked-list and return it.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you merge K sorted linked lists efficiently using a Priority Queue?
questions.hint: Push the head node of each of the K lists into a Min-Heap. Pop the minimum node, attach it to the result list, and push its next node into the heap.
commonMistakes: Pushing null list heads into the heap
Comparing node values incorrectly inside the heap data structure comparator
followUpQuestions: How would you merge these lists using Divide and Conquer, and what is its space complexity compared to the heap approach?
What if the lists are stored on external disk partitions?

questions.name: Last Stone Weight
questions.description: You are given an array of integers stones where stones[i] is the weight of the ith stone. Repeatedly smash the two heaviest stones until at most one stone remains.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you simulate a game where you repeatedly pull and modify the two largest values using a Max-Heap?
questions.hint: Insert all stone weights into a Max-Heap. Pop two largest stones, subtract their weights, and push the remainder back if non-zero.
commonMistakes: Re-sorting the array after every smash step, yielding O(n² log n) complexity
Not handling the case where the heap becomes empty
followUpQuestions: Can this problem be solved using Bucket Sort or a counting array if stone weights are bounded?
How does the time complexity change if stone weights are very large?

questions.name: Task Scheduler
questions.description: Given a characters array tasks and a cooling time n, return the minimum number of CPU intervals required to complete all tasks.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you schedule tasks with execution cooling periods to minimize total CPU execution time?
questions.hint: Greedily schedule the highest frequency task available using a Max-Heap alongside a cooling queue.
commonMistakes: Failing to account for idle CPU cycles during cooldown intervals
Not prioritizing remaining tasks by frequency count
followUpQuestions: Can you derive a pure math formula solution in O(n) time without heaps?
How would you solve this if tasks have individual execution durations instead of 1 unit?

questions.name: Ugly Number II
questions.description: An ugly number is a positive integer whose prime factors are limited to 2, 3, and 5. Given an integer n, return the nth ugly number.
questions.interviewQuestion: How do you generate the Nth ugly number efficiently using a Min-Heap or Dynamic Programming?
questions.hint: Use a Min-Heap with a Set to generate and retrieve multiples of 2, 3, and 5 in sorted order, or use three pointers DP.
commonMistakes: Pushing duplicate numbers into the Min-Heap without using a Set
Integer overflow issues when generating higher multiples of ugly numbers
followUpQuestions: How does the Three-Pointer DP approach achieve O(n) time complexity?
How would you extend this to Super Ugly Number (arbitrary prime factors)?
questions.timeComplexity: O(n log n) with Heap, O(n) with DP

questions.name: Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists
